mentions.name: CodePlusEqualsAI
mentions.description: An LLM webapp builder that performs AST-based code edits: instead of editing files directly, the LLM writes Python code (e.g., using BeautifulSoup) that is executed to parse a file such as HTML into a data structure, modify it, and output the resulting HTML. The platform also includes a marketplace where builders can publish their LLM-powered webapps and earn money on token margins (charged at 2x token rates) when people use their sites.
mentions.source_excerpt:
AST-based code edits from LLMs: https://codeplusequalsai.com

It's an LLM-webapp-builder, sure, but different from the rest! I have the LLM write python code when it needs to modify an HTML file for example (it'll use beautifulsoup; then I run the code: it parses the source into a data structure, modifies the data structure, and then outputs the resulting html).

It's also a marketplace where you can publish your llm-powered webapp, and earn $ on the token margins (I charge 2x token rates) when people use your site.

mentions.name: codeplusequalsai.com
mentions.description: A platform for AST-based code modifications from LLMs, built on the idea that having LLMs modify the structure of code may work better than writing raw code with line-or-diff replacements. It also builds a per-token-call margin into LLM-powered webapps: end users are charged 2x the provider's token costs, with 80% of the remainder going to the dev and 20% to the platform.
mentions.problem: LLMs writing raw code and doing line-or-diff replacements may not be the future of AI coding; devs building LLM-powered webapps also lack a way to earn per token call.
mentions.audience: Developers building LLM-powered webapps, who earn per token call
mentions.source_excerpt:
AST-based code modifications from LLMs: https://codeplusequalsai.com/

I'm interested in the idea that LLMs writing raw code and doing line-or-diff replacements will not be the future, but that having the LLMs modify the structure of the code may end up being the best.

Also, I think that building LLM-powered webapps should earn the dev per token call; so I've built a margin into token costs where the end user is charged 2x the provider's token costs, and then I get 20% of the remaining and the dev gets 80%.
